articles.title: In turbulent times, football brings Haiti hope
articles.summary: The security crisis has displaced more than a million people and caused thousands of deaths, affecting every sector of national life. This includes sport, in general, and football, in particular.
articles.content:
In Haiti, the sport of football creates social cohesion: despite their differences, people from all classes come together on the field. Children from wealthy families, poor backgrounds, and middle-class homes alike get the opportunity to mix by either playing for the same football team, or facing one another as opponents.

The same approach informs how players are chosen for the national team; all social categories are represented based solely on the quality of each player’s talent. Spectators have a similar experience, in that people from all walks of life cross paths to celebrate, support their teams, and share moments of victory or defeat.

Naturally, the security crisis that has displaced more than a million people internally and caused thousands of deaths over the last six years has affected every sector of national life. This includes sport in general and football, in particular, since “the beautiful game” is a passion for almost all ages and social groups in Haiti.

Despite the country’s lack of modern sports infrastructure, you can see people of every generation playing football everywhere: on school grounds, in the streets, on unpaved fields, in yards and corridors, and in sports parks across the country. For young people from poor and disadvantaged neighbourhoods, football offers an opportunity to join local semi-professional clubs and maybe even play at national level.

Since the gang violence has escalated, however, much of the country’s main infrastructure has been damaged through looting, fire, or other means, and sports facilities have not been spared. The FIFA Goal Center in Croix-des-Bouquets, for instance, which trained stars like Melchie Dumornay (Corventina) of Olympique Lyonnais in France, Nérilia Mondésir of Seattle Reign FC in the United States, and Kethna Louis of Montpellier HSC in France, was attacked, looted, and burned by the 400 Mawozo gang led by Wilson Joseph (alias Lanmò San Jou).

Likewise, the Sylvio Cator Stadium in southern Port-au-Prince, the home of Haitian national football, and the Haitian Olympic Center in Croix-des-Missions in the city's north, where many young people would train in different sports, suffered major gang attacks in February 2024 and February 2026, respectively. The area around the Sylvio Cator Stadium is controlled by two powerful gangs, one led by Renel Destina (alias “Ti Lapli” or “Kaporal Lapli”) and the other by Johnson André (alias “Izo 5 Second”). The Olympic Center area is controlled by Claudy Célestin (alias “Chen Mechan” or “Stevenson Pierre”) of the Chen Mechan (“Mean Dog,” in English) gang in Plaine-du-Cul-de-Sac, and Jeff Larose (alias Jeff Gwo Lwa) of the Taliban gang based in Canaan.

Because criminal gangs control the main roads leading to the country's Great South and Great North, the regular national championship has halted, forcing the national football league to adapt and organise a special competition so players can keep playing. Many sports parks are located in areas controlled by gangs, which makes the situation worse.

Despite all this, Haitian football is not dead. On November 18, 2025, the Grenadiers qualified for the 2026 World Cup, even though no qualifying match was played in Haiti because of the gang violence. Although the national team was eliminated in the first round of the World Cup, their participation brought joy to the Haitian people.

The sport continues to put smiles on people’s faces in Haiti. In this year’s Caribbean Football Union (CFU) U14 Challenge Series, which ended on August 23 in Punta Cana, Dominican Republic, the Haitian U14 team won the tournament with a series of brilliant performances.

They beat Trinidad and Tobago 4-1 and French Guiana 5-2, lost 1-0 to Puerto Rico (after already qualifying for the semifinals), defeated the host nation 6-1 in the semifinals, and beat Jamaica 4-0 in the final to become Division 1 champions. This victory marked Haiti’s third CFU U14 title, following their previous championship wins in 2021 and 2022. All three titles were secured during a time when the country was going through a crisis.

To help these young players participate in the tournament, the Haitian Football Federation (FHF) organised a talent detection tournament across various regions of the island, with participation from several football academies. Young footballers were enrolled in a two-month preparation camp at the Dulaire Sports Complex/Training Center, in the municipality of Ouanaminthe and, more specifically, in the communal section of Haut-Maribahoux, a border area near Dajabón in the Dominican Republic.

The young champions returned home on Monday, August 24, to a welcome reception at the diplomatic lounge of the Toussaint Louverture International Airport in Port-au-Prince, organised by the Ministry of Youth, Sports, and Civic Action (MJSAC).

During the ceremony, the Minister of Sports highlighted individual performances, including Jerry Petit-Homme, who scored a goal just four or five seconds into the match against the Dominican Republic — one of the fastest goals in football history. Wensley Dumorné was named the Best Player of Division 1, and Jodley Sheeckensley Delmas was named top scorer, with seven goals.

Team captain Cedric Clairemond shared a warm message with Haitian football fans, on behalf of all the players:

Moun yo mèsi anpil pou lamou nou, jodi a nou chanpyon nou ba nou koup la, mwen fyè anpil paske mwen reprezante peyi'm antan ke kapitèn, sa fè de mwa n ap prepare, nou te motive pou sa, tout objektif la se te chanpyon jodi a nou fè'l, nou swete pou nou rejwi de koup la, ti grenadye yo ap vini pou nou monte pi wo.

Thank you everyone so much for your love. Today we are champions and we bring you the trophy. I am very proud to represent my country as captain. We prepared for two months and were very motivated. The goal was to become champions, and today we did it. We hope you enjoy this trophy; the young Grenadiers are coming to reach even higher levels.

Sports Minister Phytagore Dumas stated his commitment to supporting these young players in their education and personal growth. According to a statement from his ministry, the young Grenadiers won on the field, and it is now up to the nation to support them towards a future worthy of their talent.

The Haitian Football Federation echoed this sentiment:

Aktivite jodi a se te pou temwanye yo lanmou ak sipò, pou renouvle angajman nou pou kontinye batay pou leve nivo foutbòl la nan peyi a epi garanti relèv la. Objektif la pa t lòt, se mize sou jenès la jodi a pou reyalize rèv demen yo.

Today’s event was to show them love and support, and to renew our commitment to keep fighting to raise the level of football in the country and secure the future. The objective was simple: invest in today’s youth to achieve tomorrow’s dreams.

Haiti’s U17 national team is currently preparing at Parc Sainte-Claire in Delmas for the 20th edition of the FIFA U-17 World Cup in Qatar, training and playing friendly matches against local teams to get ready for the tournament, which takes place from November 19 to December 13. Meanwhile, the U20s narrowly missed qualification for the FIFA U-20 World Cup in Chile. On August 31, however, the same team qualified for the men’s football tournament of the 2027 Pan American Games, to be held in Lima, Peru. Haiti earned its spot as the highest-ranked Caribbean team following its performance in the recent Concacaf U-20 Championship.

Yet, because of the ongoing violence, especially in the metropolitan area of Port-au-Prince, Haiti itself cannot celebrate as it would like. Even with the U14s’ great performance, the joy did not last long. On the night of August 24, fewer than 24 hours after their victory, armed gangs from the criminal group Viv Ansanm killed around 47 people and kidnapped more than 30 others, including young girls, women, and seniors in the municipality of Kenscoff, a mountain town near the capital.

In spite of the challenges, good things keep happening every day in the country. You can see it in culture, art, farming projects, entrepreneurship and sport, especially in parts of the country not under gang control. Perhaps that is football’s most enduring lesson — that in spite of obstacles, you must keep moving forward.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights how football in Haiti fosters social cohesion and hope amid severe national crises and gang violence. Despite infrastructure damage and security challenges, young Haitian football teams achieve significant victories, including qualifying for the World Cup and winning regional tournaments. The story demonstrates tangible positive impact on youth development, national pride, and community resilience, with broad societal significance beyond sports. The detailed context and examples provide a substantive, inspiring narrative of perseverance and unity.
articles.personality_title: Football unites Haiti amid crisis and brings young champions hope
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Haiti faces a severe security crisis with gang violence that has displaced over a million people and damaged important sports facilities. This crisis affects all parts of life, including football, a sport loved by many Haitians.

**What happened** – Despite the challenges, Haitian football continues to bring people together. Young players from all social backgrounds train and compete, showing talent and teamwork. Recently, Haiti’s under-14 football team won the Caribbean Football Union (CFU) U14 Challenge Series in the Dominican Republic, marking their third title during difficult times. They were welcomed home with celebrations and praise from government officials and sports leaders. Meanwhile, Haiti’s national teams are preparing for upcoming international events, including the FIFA U-17 World Cup and the Pan American Games.

**Impact** – Football in Haiti goes beyond sport; it creates connections between people from different backgrounds and offers hope to young players and communities. Even with damaged stadiums and gang violence, football remains a source of pride and joy. The success of youth teams shows how investing in young talent can inspire a nation and provide opportunities despite hardship.

**What’s next step** – The Haitian Football Federation and government plan to continue supporting young players through education and training. The focus is on building the future of football in Haiti and helping these athletes reach higher levels. Upcoming tournaments will test the teams further, and efforts to protect sports facilities and communities remain crucial.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Despite violence and hardship, football in Haiti brings people together and gives young players a chance to shine and build hope for the future.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le football unit Haïti en pleine crise et offre de l’espoir aux jeunes champions
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Haïti traverse une grave crise de sécurité avec la violence des gangs qui a déplacé plus d’un million de personnes et endommagé des infrastructures sportives importantes. Cette crise touche tous les aspects de la vie, y compris le football, un sport très apprécié des Haïtiens.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Malgré ces difficultés, le football haïtien continue de rassembler les gens. De jeunes joueurs de tous horizons s’entraînent et jouent ensemble, montrant leur talent et leur esprit d’équipe. Récemment, l’équipe haïtienne des moins de 14 ans a remporté la série de défis de l’Union de football des Caraïbes (CFU) en République dominicaine, décrochant leur troisième titre en période difficile. Leur retour a été célébré avec enthousiasme par les autorités et les dirigeants sportifs. Par ailleurs, les équipes nationales se préparent pour des compétitions internationales comme la Coupe du Monde U-17 de la FIFA et les Jeux Panaméricains.

**Impact** – Le football en Haïti dépasse le simple sport ; il crée des liens entre des personnes de milieux différents et offre de l’espoir aux jeunes joueurs et aux communautés. Malgré les stades endommagés et la violence des gangs, le football reste une source de fierté et de joie. Le succès des équipes de jeunes montre que l’investissement dans le talent des jeunes peut inspirer une nation et offrir des opportunités malgré les difficultés.

**Prochaine étape** – La Fédération haïtienne de football et le gouvernement prévoient de continuer à soutenir les jeunes joueurs par l’éducation et la formation. L’objectif est de construire l’avenir du football en Haïti et d’aider ces athlètes à atteindre des niveaux plus élevés. Les prochains tournois seront des défis importants, et la protection des infrastructures sportives et des communautés reste essentielle.

**En une phrase** – Malgré la violence et les difficultés, le football en Haïti unit les gens et donne aux jeunes joueurs une chance de briller et de construire un avenir plein d’espoir.
articles.personality_title_es: El fútbol une a Haití en medio de la crisis y da esperanza a jóvenes campeones
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Haití enfrenta una grave crisis de seguridad con violencia de pandillas que ha desplazado a más de un millón de personas y dañado instalaciones deportivas importantes. Esta crisis afecta todos los aspectos de la vida, incluido el fútbol, un deporte muy querido en Haití.

**Qué pasó** – A pesar de las dificultades, el fútbol haitiano sigue uniendo a la gente. Jóvenes jugadores de diferentes orígenes entrenan y compiten mostrando talento y trabajo en equipo. Recientemente, el equipo sub-14 de Haití ganó la Serie de Desafíos de la Unión de Fútbol del Caribe (CFU) en República Dominicana, logrando su tercer título durante tiempos difíciles. Fueron recibidos con celebraciones y reconocimiento de autoridades y líderes deportivos. Mientras tanto, los equipos nacionales se preparan para eventos internacionales como la Copa Mundial Sub-17 de la FIFA y los Juegos Panamericanos.

**Impacto** – El fútbol en Haití es más que un deporte; crea conexiones entre personas de distintos orígenes y ofrece esperanza a los jóvenes y sus comunidades. A pesar de los daños en los estadios y la violencia de las pandillas, el fútbol sigue siendo una fuente de orgullo y alegría. El éxito de los equipos juveniles demuestra cómo invertir en talento joven puede inspirar a una nación y abrir oportunidades en medio de las dificultades.

**Próximo paso** – La Federación Haitiana de Fútbol y el gobierno planean seguir apoyando a los jóvenes jugadores con educación y entrenamiento. El objetivo es construir el futuro del fútbol en Haití y ayudar a estos atletas a alcanzar niveles más altos. Los próximos torneos serán una prueba importante, y proteger las instalaciones deportivas y las comunidades sigue siendo fundamental.

**Una frase clave** – A pesar de la violencia y las dificultades, el fútbol en Haití une a la gente y da a los jóvenes la oportunidad de brillar y construir un futuro esperanzador.

articles.title: Ancient cave art discovery suggests first known humans in Ireland walked over from Wales
articles.summary: During the most recent Ice Age, researchers believe there was a "lost land bridge" between Wales and Ireland.
articles.content:
Researchers believe the first known humans to set foot on Ireland thousands of years ago were most likely from Wales, following the "exciting" discovery of ancient cave art.

During the most recent Ice Age, when much of the British Isles were beneath a vast continental glacier, the depleted sea levels opened a "lost land bridge" between modern-day Pembrokeshire and the south-east tip of Ireland, around Rosslare.

According to rock expert Dr George Nash, from Liverpool University, the opportunities presented by this pathway would have been too good for hunter gatherers to ignore.

Now, alongside an international team of experts, Nash has located eight cave sites in south-west Ireland featuring rock art dating back from at least 15,000 years ago, around 5,000 years before the previous oldest example of humans in Ireland.

Nash, who coordinated the Lost Land Bridge Project, said there would have been a forested and grassland plateau around 46 miles (76 km) coast-to-coast.

With summertime temperatures typically -10°C to -20°C, Nash said the pathway would have supported wild horses, mammoth, bison, reindeer and other large herbivores, which fed off the hardy sedges, mosses and lichens growing through the fertile, but near-frozen soil.

Nash said he had always believed - from what he had gleaned throughout his career about human movement during the period - that it was inconceivable that people would not have utilised the opportunity the pathway presented.

This led him to assemble his multi-disciplinary team of experts from University College Dublin and the University of Adelaide, along with academics from Dubai, Wales and Portugal.
articles.reasoning: The discovery of ancient cave art and evidence of a lost land bridge offers significant new insights into early human migration and history in Ireland, which is inspiring and broadens our understanding of human prehistory. The story is focused, detailed, and involves a meaningful archaeological breakthrough with broad cultural and scientific interest.
articles.personality_title: Ancient cave art reveals how first humans reached Ireland from Wales
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Thousands of years ago, during the last Ice Age, much of the British Isles were covered by glaciers. Lower sea levels created a land bridge between Wales and Ireland, which scientists have called a "lost land bridge."

**What happened** – Researchers, led by Dr. George Nash from Liverpool University, found ancient cave art in southwest Ireland. This art dates back at least 15,000 years, about 5,000 years earlier than previously known human activity in Ireland. The discovery supports the idea that early humans crossed from Wales to Ireland using the land bridge.

**Impact** – This discovery changes what we know about how and when humans first arrived in Ireland. It shows that early humans used this natural route to move between lands, hunting animals like mammoths and reindeer along the way. The cave art also gives us a rare glimpse into their lives and environment during a very cold period.

**What's next step** – The Lost Land Bridge Project team will continue studying these cave sites and the surrounding area. They hope to learn more about the people who made the art and how they lived. This could help us understand more about human migration and survival during the Ice Age.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Ancient cave art and a lost land bridge reveal that the first humans likely walked from Wales to Ireland over 15,000 years ago, reshaping our knowledge of early human travel in the region.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une ancienne peinture rupestre révèle comment les premiers humains sont arrivés en Irlande depuis le Pays de Galles
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Il y a des milliers d'années, pendant la dernière période glaciaire, une grande partie des îles britanniques était recouverte de glaciers. Le niveau de la mer étant plus bas, un pont terrestre appelé « pont terrestre perdu » reliait le Pays de Galles à l'Irlande.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs, dirigés par le Dr George Nash de l'université de Liverpool, ont découvert des peintures rupestres anciennes dans le sud-ouest de l'Irlande. Ces peintures datent d'au moins 15 000 ans, soit environ 5 000 ans avant les premières traces humaines connues en Irlande. Cette découverte confirme que les premiers humains ont traversé ce pont terrestre.

**Impact** – Cette découverte modifie notre compréhension de l'arrivée des humains en Irlande. Elle montre que les premiers humains ont utilisé cette voie naturelle pour se déplacer, chassant des animaux comme le mammouth et le renne. Les peintures offrent aussi un aperçu rare de leur vie et de leur environnement pendant cette période froide.

**Étape suivante** – L'équipe du projet Lost Land Bridge va continuer à étudier ces sites et leurs environs. Ils espèrent en apprendre davantage sur les personnes qui ont créé ces œuvres et leur mode de vie. Cela pourrait enrichir notre connaissance des migrations humaines et de la survie durant l'ère glaciaire.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des peintures rupestres anciennes et un pont terrestre perdu montrent que les premiers humains ont probablement marché du Pays de Galles à l'Irlande il y a plus de 15 000 ans, changeant notre vision des premiers déplacements humains dans la région.
articles.personality_title_es: Arte rupestre antiguo revela cómo los primeros humanos llegaron a Irlanda desde Gales
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Hace miles de años, durante la última Edad de Hielo, gran parte de las islas británicas estaba cubierta por glaciares. Los niveles bajos del mar crearon un puente terrestre llamado "puente perdido" entre Gales e Irlanda.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores, liderados por el Dr. George Nash de la Universidad de Liverpool, encontraron arte rupestre antiguo en el suroeste de Irlanda. Este arte tiene al menos 15,000 años, unos 5,000 años más antiguo que las evidencias humanas conocidas anteriormente en Irlanda. El hallazgo apoya la idea de que los primeros humanos cruzaron de Gales a Irlanda usando este puente terrestre.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento cambia lo que sabemos sobre cómo y cuándo llegaron los humanos a Irlanda. Muestra que usaron esta ruta natural para moverse, cazando animales como mamuts y renos. El arte rupestre también nos da una visión rara sobre sus vidas y el ambiente durante un período muy frío.

**Próximo paso** – El equipo del Proyecto Lost Land Bridge seguirá estudiando estos sitios y el área cercana. Esperan aprender más sobre las personas que hicieron el arte y cómo vivían. Esto podría ayudar a entender mejor la migración humana y la supervivencia durante la Edad de Hielo.

**Resumen en una frase** – El arte rupestre antiguo y un puente terrestre perdido revelan que los primeros humanos probablemente caminaron de Gales a Irlanda hace más de 15,000 años, cambiando nuestro conocimiento sobre los primeros viajes humanos en la región.
